sections.title: CliffCompaction: Cost-Efficient Compaction for Long-Horizon Coding Agents
sections.abstract: The paper proposes an autocompaction method that only truncates or drops original content, reporting up to 50% lower cost while maintaining or improving coding-agent performance on Terminal-Bench and KernelBench.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors claim that non-rewriting compaction avoids cumulative context drift and improves test-time scaling efficiency.
sections.caveat: The evidence is a preprint's reported benchmark evaluation and may not generalize across harnesses.

sections.title: Grow the Harness, Not the Context: From Strategy-Free Scaffolds to Reusable Specialist Agents
sections.abstract: Growing Harness learns reusable executable control code from task failures, reducing repeated LLM decisions and reporting lower cost across two web-agent benchmarks.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors claim persistent program growth moves recurring control into reusable code.
sections.caveat: Results cover two web-agent benchmarks and three deployment models.

sections.title: SWE-Serve: Benchmarking Agentic Engineering For Production Inference Serving
sections.abstract: SWE-Serve introduces 53 repository-grounded tasks for production inference-serving changes with hidden functional, regression, end-to-end, and performance tests.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors claim E2E tests expose a production-correctness gap.
sections.caveat: The benchmark is derived from SGLang and limited hardware settings.

sections.title: Recursive self-improvement of AI research agents
sections.abstract: AIDE² recursively edits and benchmarks its own research-agent code, reporting transfer to held-out engineering and weather-forecasting tasks.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors claim recursive self-improvement can improve research efficiency and transfer beyond selection tasks.
sections.caveat: The abstract reports one autonomous run and leaves robustness to seeds and budgets open.

sections.title: Dual-Frontier: When Can an Agent Trust Its World Model?
sections.abstract: Dual-Frontier formalizes failure attribution between an agent decision rule and world model, then admits model-guided decisions only when predicted advantage exceeds certified model-error bounds.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors claim a verify-then-promote rule with non-decreasing-return guarantees for admitted decisions.
sections.caveat: The guarantees depend on calibration and verification assumptions.

sections.title: JEV-as-a-Judge: Accept When Confident, Escalate When Unsure
sections.abstract: The paper evaluates a low-cost decision-only judge and confidence-based cascade against stronger judges with blinded human adjudication.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors claim confidence-based escalation retains 99% of comparator accuracy at lower cost.
sections.caveat: Larger gaps occur on derivation checking and elaborate wrong answers.

sections.title: FIRE: Failure-Informed Runtime Engineering for Reliable Language-Model Agents
sections.abstract: FIRE applies targeted runtime instructions and action denials at states preceding failures, reporting higher repeated success on Terminal-Bench 2.1.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors claim runtime policies make existing capabilities more repeatable.
sections.caveat: Generalization beyond the evaluated Terminal-Bench setup is not shown.
